segments.visual: The code panel types three lines, slow, fast and kept: one count per clinic, written three ways. A wall counter sits in the corner, blank.

sentences.text: Here's one question written three ways: patients per clinic. Every version gives the same answer.
Which one runs fastest? Make a guess before they run.

segments.visual: Three cards, one per line; each card's wall counter fills in from Spark's own plan: two, one, one.

sentences.text: Here's a clue you can read straight from Spark's plan: how many walls each one builds. Two, one, and one.

segments.visual: Series wordmark, Spark, Visually; Part II, Why jobs are slow; the episode title.

sentences.text: Welcome to Spark, Visually. Part Two: why jobs are slow.
Today: counting walls.

segments.visual: Five cards: filter, select, withColumn, union, coalesce. For each, arrows run straight down, tray to tray; the wall counter stays at 0, and each runs as one stage. The union card notes: in SQL that is UNION ALL; plain UNION also removes duplicates, and that is a wall.

sentences.text: Some steps send each input pile whole to one output pile. A filter, a select, a new column: each pile is worked where it lies.
Union just stacks two tables' piles, and coalesce merges neighbours where they stand. No wall, so each runs as a single stage.

segments.visual: Six cards: groupBy, distinct, join, repartition, a window over each clinic, orderBy. Each lights Episode 5's all-to-all lattice across the benches; the wall counter ticks: 1, 1, 2 for the join, 1, 1, 1. The join card shows its hint, .hint("merge"): copying the small table instead is Episode 8.

sentences.text: Other steps need rows from every pile: a count per clinic, distinct rows, a join, a re-deal, a window over each clinic, a sort. Each one builds a wall.
A join that deals out both tables, as this hint asks, builds a wall on each side.

segments.visual: orderBy's card: the shelf is read twice, once by the sampling job and once by the map stage, then one wall. Beside it, sortWithinPartitions: no wall.

sentences.text: Sorting needs care. orderBy sorts the whole table: one wall, plus an extra job that reads the table once more, to sample the rows and choose the ranges.
To sort each pile where it lies, there's sortWithinPartitions, with no wall at all.

segments.visual: Line 4 types: slow.explain(). Two Exchange lines light: RoundRobinPartitioning(200), then hashpartitioning(clinic, 200). Slow's wall counter: two. A caption: on Databricks Photon compute, a wall can also appear as a PhotonShuffleExchangeSink line; count those too.

sentences.text: You don't have to guess. Ask for the plan, and count the lines that begin with Exchange. Each one is a wall.
Slow has two: a re-deal into 200 piles, then the deal by clinic that the count needs anyway.
sentences.say: Slow has two: a re-deal into two hundred piles, then the deal by clinic that the count needs anyway.

segments.visual: Fast's and kept's plans: one Exchange each. Kept's count needs no second wall: its rows are already dealt by clinic.

sentences.text: Fast has one. So does kept: it deals by clinic up front, so the count finds each clinic's rows already in one place.

segments.visual: Line 5 glows: all three run, on the cast ten thousand times over. A ledger per version: its walls, and the rows crossing each.

sentences.text: Now run all three on the cast ten thousand times over, just over a million rows.
Slow sends every row across its first wall, then 1,000 partial counts across its second.
sentences.say: Slow sends every row across its first wall, then a thousand partial counts across its second.

sentences.text: Fast sends only partial counts: 40 small rows, one per clinic per pile. Kept sends every row, once.
sentences.say: Fast sends only partial counts: forty small rows, one per clinic per pile. Kept sends every row, once.

segments.visual: Bytes written per version, on this table: fast 2.9 kB, kept 164 kB, slow 404 kB.

sentences.text: In bytes, fast wins by far, then kept, then slow.
Fast wins because there are only five clinics, so the partial counts are tiny. With many more groups, they shrink less.

segments.visual: Kept's deal by clinic, with later steps that need clinic lining up behind it, no new wall for them. Beside it, slow's round-robin deal, which no later step needs.

sentences.text: So why deal up front at all? Only when several later steps need rows dealt by the same key: then one wall serves them all. That's episode 17.
sentences.say: So why deal up front at all? Only when several later steps need rows dealt by the same key: then one wall serves them all. That's episode seventeen.

sentences.text: A re-deal into 200 piles, just to be safe, helps no step here.
sentences.say: A re-deal into two hundred piles, just to be safe, helps no step here.

segments.visual: A wide step with no new wall: rows already dealt the right way. A small table copied to every bench, a hint of Episode 8.

sentences.text: And a wide step doesn't always build a new wall: not when the rows are already dealt the right way, and, as you'll see, not when a small table is copied instead.

segments.visual: Three recap cards: narrow steps work each pile where it lies; wide steps build a wall; count the Exchange lines.

sentences.text: Let's gather it up.
Narrow steps work each pile where it lies. Wide steps build a wall, unless the rows are already in place, and the plan's Exchange lines count them.
Fewer walls, and less across each: that's a cost you can read from the plan.

segments.visual: A join's two walls; the next episode's title: Send the small table.

sentences.text: A join is the commonest wall of all. Must it be one? Next time: send the small table.

segments.visual: Series end card with the next episode title.

sentences.text: This has been Spark, Visually. Thanks for watching the cluster with us.
